name: Intravenous ascorbic acid

lead: Intravenous ascorbic acid is vitamin C delivered directly into a vein rather than swallowed. It reaches blood levels that oral dosing cannot, and complementary and alternative medicine practitioners offer it [1]. People interested in appearance seek it because vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen formation, the protein underpinning skin firmness [2].
Most published research is on critically ill patients, where meta-analyses report a trend toward lower mortality in sepsis [3][4]. Trials examining skin appearance after IV vitamin C were not found.

paras: A clinician places an IV line and runs the vitamin C solution in over a period of time, sometimes as part of a mixed 'drip'. It is offered at wellness and integrative clinics and in hospitals for medical uses.

Large doses can upset the stomach and cause flushing and headache [2]. Case reports and a scoping review document harms from high-dose IV therapy [5], and IV vitamin C has been reported to cause falsely high glucose readings on some meters [6]. Anyone considering it would discuss it with a clinician.

social.title: IV Vitamin C reduces mortality in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome patients

chain: High-dose vitamin C infused into the bloodstream
Raises plasma vitamin C and antioxidant availability
Collagen support and skin health, as claimed by providers
angle.text: Practitioners and clients describe IV vitamin C as a route to brighter, healthier-looking skin by supplying a collagen cofactor and antioxidant. This is a stated rationale rather than a result shown in cosmetic trials.

lead: Intravenous ascorbic acid, or IV vitamin C, is the administration of vitamin C by infusion. IV dosing produces concentrations far above those reached by oral intake, at which vitamin C is described as acting as a pro-oxidant [1]. A survey of attendees at US complementary and alternative medicine conferences found practitioners using it, with sales tracked from major distributors [2].

The interest for appearance rests on a chain: vitamin C is a cofactor for enzymes that stabilize collagen, which gives skin, vessels and scar tissue their structure, and deficiency (scurvy) produces skin spots and bleeding under the skin [1]. Clinics promoting IV vitamin C for skin glow and recovery draw on this reasoning.
Published clinical work concerns medical settings, chiefly critical illness and sepsis [3][4][5], COVID-19 [6], and cancer adjunct therapy [7].

paras: Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin and a cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine, steps collagen needs to form its stable structure [1]. Given intravenously it bypasses the limits of intestinal absorption and yields non-physiological blood concentrations, at which it has shown toxicity to cancer cells in laboratory descriptions [1].

Complementary and alternative medicine practitioners offer IV vitamin C; a 2010 survey of conference attendees documented how widely it was used and what side effects practitioners had seen [2]. Skin-brightening and anti-aging marketing is common in the wellness sector, framed around vitamin C's roles in collagen and antioxidant defense [1].

A 2022 meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials in 2,490 critically ill patients reported a trend toward lower mortality, with a significant reduction in high-dose and monotherapy subgroups, and no increase in treatment-related adverse events [3]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 sepsis trials reported trends toward lower mortality and improved organ-failure scores after more than 72 hours of treatment [4]. A 2021 review of 53 studies also examined critically ill patients, noting concern about kidney toxicity raised by case reports [8]. Studies in COVID-19 were mixed: of six studies on lung function, three found improvement and three found none [6]. Reviews also consider IV vitamin C as a cancer adjunct [7].

Vitamin C is generally well tolerated; large oral doses cause stomach upset, headache, sleep problems and flushing [1]. A scoping review collected reports of harm from high-dose IV therapy in adults [9]. Case reports describe infusion-related pseudohyperglycemia on glucose meters [10].

No studies found on IV vitamin C for skin appearance. Human trials exist in sepsis, septic shock, vasoplegia and COVID-19, summarized above [3][4][5][6]. A 2022 septic shock trial and a 2023 vasoplegia trial are among those registered in the literature [5][11].
